sections.title: The best line through a cloud

blocks.html: Bigger apartments cost more rent, roughly. "Roughly" is the interesting part: the points don't sit on a line. So which line is best? The classic answer: the line that makes the squared vertical misses as small as possible in total. In the simulation those squares are real squares. Shrink them.

blocks.name: ps-regress
blocks.title: Least squares, literally
blocks.goal: Use the sliders to get within 5% of the smallest possible total square area by hand, then press Add outlier.
blocks.intro: Each amber square's side is a point's vertical miss (its residual). The number at the top left is their total area. Try to make it as small as you can.

blocks.q: Why does one far-away outlier move the least-squares line so much?

opts.t: Outliers have more weight in the formula by design
Its miss gets squared, so a miss 5 times bigger counts 25 times as much, and the line tilts to reduce it
The line has to pass through every point
It doesn't; least squares ignores outliers

blocks.why: Squaring is what makes the maths neat (one exact best line), and also what makes it sensitive: a single big residual can dominate the total. Always plot your data before trusting a fitted line.

blocks.html:
Do two variables rise together? Look at each point's distance from the averages: (x − x̄) and (y − ȳ). When both are above average, or both below, their product is positive. The average of those products is the covariance. Its size depends on the units (cm vs m changes it), so we divide by both standard deviations to get the correlation r, which is always between −1 and 1:

  • r = 1: a perfect rising line; r = −1: a perfect falling line;
  • r = 0: no straight-line relationship (there could still be a curve!).

blocks.code:
x = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], float)
print(np.corrcoef(x, 2 * x + 1)[0, 1])
print(np.corrcoef(x, -x)[0, 1])
print(round(np.corrcoef(x, (x - 3) ** 2)[0, 1], 6))

blocks.html: The last one is a perfect relationship (a parabola) with correlation 0. Correlation only sees straight lines.

blocks.title: correlation
blocks.prompt: Write correlation(x, y) from the definition: the sum of (x - mean_x) * (y - mean_y) divided by sqrt(sum((x - mean_x)**2) * sum((y - mean_y)**2)). Don't use np.corrcoef (the tests compare against it).
blocks.tests:
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
a, b = rng.normal(size=200), rng.normal(size=200)
c = a + 0.5 * b
assert abs(correlation(a, c) - np.corrcoef(a, c)[0, 1]) < 1e-12, "matches numpy"
assert abs(correlation([1, 2, 3], [30, 20, 10]) + 1) < 1e-12, "a perfect falling line: -1"
assert abs(correlation(a, 100 * c + 7) - correlation(a, c)) < 1e-12, "changing units doesn't change the correlation"
hints: Centre both arrays first (dx = x - x.mean()), then it's one sum on top and a square root of two sums underneath.

def correlation(x, y):

blocks.html: Ice-cream sales and drownings are strongly correlated. Ice cream doesn't cause drowning: hot weather drives both. A hidden variable that moves both is a confounder. Others: children's shoe size correlates with reading skill (age), hospitals correlate with deaths (sick people go there). To show causation you need an experiment (randomise who gets the treatment, chapter 9) or very careful reasoning about every confounder.

blocks.q: A study finds that people who drink more coffee live longer. What's the most careful conclusion?

opts.t: Coffee makes you live longer
Living longer makes you drink coffee
Coffee drinking and longevity are associated; something else (income, health, habits) could drive both, so this alone doesn't show coffee causes it
The study must be wrong

blocks.why: Observational data shows association. Healthier, wealthier people might both drink more coffee and live longer. Only a randomised experiment (or strong causal reasoning) separates cause from confounding.

blocks.html:
For a line y = a + b·x, minimising the total squared residual Σ (yᵢ − a − b·xᵢ)² with calculus gives a beautiful answer:

b = Σ (x − x̄)(y − ȳ) / Σ (x − x̄)² a = ȳ − b·x̄

So the slope is "how x and y move together" divided by "how much x moves", and the line always passes through the point of averages (x̄, ȳ).

blocks.tests:

assert abs(a - 1) < 1e-12 and abs(b - 2) < 1e-12, "points exactly on y = 1 + 2x give back a = 1, b = 2"
lines: dx, dy = x - x.mean(), y - y.mean()

blocks.title: fit_line
blocks.prompt: Write fit_line(x, y) returning (a, b) for the least-squares line y = a + b·x, using the formulas above.
blocks.tests:
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
x = rng.uniform(0, 10, 50)

assert abs(a - pa) < 1e-9 and abs(b - pb) < 1e-9, "matches np.polyfit"

hints: Centre both, slope is the sum of products over the sum of squares of the centred x, then the intercept from the averages.
blocks.starter:
def fit_line(x, y):
    return 0.0, 0.0
blocks.solution:
def fit_line(x, y):
    x, y = np.asarray(x, float), np.asarray(y, float)
    dx, dy = x - x.mean(), y - y.mean()
    b = (dx * dy).sum() / (dx ** 2).sum()
    return y.mean() - b * x.mean(), b

blocks.html:
After fitting, look at the residuals (actual − predicted). They should look like shapeless noise. A curve or a funnel in the residuals means the straight-line model is missing something.

R² says what fraction of the variation in y the line explains:

R² = 1 − Σ residual² / Σ (y − ȳ)²

R² = 1 is a perfect fit; R² = 0 means the line does no better than predicting ȳ for everyone. For a single straight line, R² is exactly r².

blocks.title: r_squared_bug
blocks.prompt: r_squared(y, predicted) gives values above 1 for decent fits. Fix the formula.
blocks.tests:

assert r_squared(y, y) == 1, "a perfect prediction explains everything"
assert abs(r_squared(y, np.full(4, y.mean()))) < 1e-12, "predicting the average for everyone explains nothing: R² = 0"
assert 0 < r_squared(y, np.array([1.2, 1.9, 3.1, 3.8])) < 1, "a decent fit is between 0 and 1"
hints: R² is the fraction of variation explained: one minus the fraction left over.
blocks.starter:
def r_squared(y, predicted):
    y, predicted = np.asarray(y, float), np.asarray(predicted, float)
    ss_res = ((y - predicted) ** 2).sum()
    ss_tot = ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum()
    return 1 + ss_res / ss_tot
blocks.solution:
def r_squared(y, predicted):
    y, predicted = np.asarray(y, float), np.asarray(predicted, float)
    ss_res = ((y - predicted) ** 2).sum()
    ss_tot = ((y - y.mean()) ** 2).sum()
    return 1 - ss_res / ss_tot

blocks.solution:
def line_and_r2(x, y):
    x, y = np.asarray(x, float), np.asarray(y, float)
    dx, dy = x - x.mean(), y - y.mean()
    b = (dx * dy).sum() / (dx ** 2).sum()
    a = y.mean() - b * x.mean()
    res = y - (a + b * x)
    return a, b, 1 - (res ** 2).sum() / (dy ** 2).sum()

blocks.q: Explain what "least squares" means and name two ways a regression line can mislead you.
blocks.a: Among all straight lines, least squares picks the one with the smallest total of squared vertical misses: each point's error is squared and the squares are added. It can mislead when (1) an outlier, because squaring makes big misses dominate and drags the line toward one strange point, and (2) when you read the slope as cause and effect: a confounder can make two things move together without one causing the other. It also only captures straight-line patterns, so always plot the data and the residuals.

chapters.title: Bayesian inference
chapters.tagline: Treat an unknown number as a belief, and let every new piece of data reshape it
goals: Describe a belief about an unknown quantity as a distribution (the prior)
Update it with data using posterior ∝ prior × likelihood, on a grid
Use the Beta–binomial shortcut for yes/no data
Read a credible interval and say how it differs from a confidence interval
Rank items with few ratings fairly using a Bayesian average

blocks.html:
In chapter 3, Bayes' rule updated the probability of one yes/no hypothesis (is the patient ill?). Now the unknown is a number: the chance p that a coin lands heads, the click rate of an ad, the defect rate of a factory. Instead of one probability we keep a whole row of them, one for every possible value of p. That row is a belief.

Two people watch the same coin. Ada has no opinion. Bo is sure the coin favours tails. Flip it and watch.

blocks.name: ps-posterior
blocks.title: Two priors, one coin
blocks.goal: Flip until Ada's and Bo's average beliefs are within 0.03 of each other.
blocks.intro: Each bar is how strongly a person believes the coin's heads-chance is that value (0 on the left, 1 on the right). The coloured bars are their 90% credible interval.

blocks.q: Bo started out very sure the coin favoured tails. Why did his belief still end up near Ada's?

opts.t: Bayes' rule ignores the prior
Each flip multiplies in more evidence; after many flips the likelihood is so sharp that it outweighs any reasonable prior
Bo changed his mind on purpose
The coin changed its bias

blocks.why: The prior counts like a fixed number of imaginary flips. Real flips keep piling up, so eventually they dominate. Only a prior that says "impossible" (a bar at exactly zero) can never be overturned, which is why careful Bayesians avoid zeros.

blocks.html:
Pick a grid of possible values for p. For each one:

  1. prior: how believable it was before the data;
  2. likelihood: how probable the data is if p were that value. For h heads and t tails it's p^h · (1 − p)^t;
  3. posterior = prior × likelihood, then divide by the total so it adds to 1.

That's all of Bayesian inference. Everything else is about doing step 3 faster.

blocks.code:
grid = np.array([0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
prior = np.array([1, 1, 1]) / 3
like = grid ** 2 * (1 - grid) ** 0      # we saw 2 heads, 0 tails
post = prior * like
post = post / post.sum()
print(post.round(3))

blocks.html: After two heads, 0.75 is nine times as believable as 0.25, because 0.75² / 0.25² = 9.

blocks.html:
For yes/no data there's a famous shortcut. If the prior has the shape of a Beta(a, b) distribution, the posterior after h heads and t tails is simply Beta(a + h, b + t). You can read a and b as "imaginary heads and tails I'm pretending I've already seen":

  • Beta(1, 1) is flat (Ada);
  • Beta(4, 12) is like having seen 4 heads and 12 tails (a Bo-ish prior, mean 0.25);
  • the posterior mean is (a + h) / (a + b + h + t).

w = grid ** (4 + 30 - 1) * (1 - grid) ** (12 + 10 - 1)

hints: Heads are evidence for a bigger p, so they belong with a.

blocks.html: A 90% credible interval is a range that holds 90% of the posterior: "given my prior and the data, I'm 90% sure p is in here". That is the sentence people wish a confidence interval meant. A confidence interval (chapter 8) is a statement about the method: 90% of intervals built this way catch the truth. With a flat prior and lots of data the two usually come out almost the same; with little data or a strong prior they can differ a lot.

blocks.prompt: Write credible_interval(grid, post, level=0.9) returning (lo, hi): the grid values where the running total of post first reaches (1 - level) / 2 and 1 - (1 - level) / 2. Use np.cumsum and np.searchsorted.

assert 0.61 < lo < 0.64 and 0.76 < hi < 0.78, f"70 heads, 30 tails on a flat prior: about (0.62, 0.77); got ({lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f})"
lo2, hi2 = credible_interval(g, post, 0.5)
assert lo < lo2 < hi2 < hi, "a 50% interval sits inside the 90% one"
hints: c = np.cumsum(post); np.searchsorted(c, x) is the first index where the running total reaches x.
blocks.starter:
def credible_interval(grid, post, level=0.9):
    return grid[0], grid[-1]
blocks.solution:
def credible_interval(grid, post, level=0.9):
    c = np.cumsum(post)
    tail = (1 - level) / 2
    return grid[np.searchsorted(c, tail)], grid[np.searchsorted(c, 1 - tail)]

blocks.q: After 7 heads in 10 flips with a flat prior, the 90% credible interval for p is about (0.45, 0.86). Which statement is correct?

opts.t: Given the flat prior and these flips, there's a 90% probability that p is between 0.45 and 0.86
90% of future flips will be between 0.45 and 0.86
p is 0.7 for sure; the interval is just rounding
If you repeated the experiment, 90% of the time you'd get 7 heads

blocks.why: A credible interval is a direct probability statement about the unknown, conditional on the prior. That's its big advantage, and its cost: someone with a different prior would report a different interval.

blocks.q: Explain how Bayesian inference updates a belief about an unknown number, and why two people with different priors end up agreeing.
blocks.a: Write down a belief about the unknown as a distribution over its possible values (the prior). For each value, compute how likely the observed data would be (the likelihood). Multiply prior by likelihood and rescale to get the posterior: values that explain the data well gain belief. With few data points the prior matters a lot; but each new observation multiplies in more evidence, the likelihood gets sharper, and it eventually swamps any prior that doesn't rule the truth out completely, so people with different reasonable priors converge.

chapters.title: Markov chains and MCMC
chapters.tagline: Random walks with short memories, and how a clever walk can sample any shape
goals: Model a system that hops between states with a transition matrix
Push a distribution forward in time and find where it settles (the stationary distribution)
Rank web pages with PageRank, a Markov chain in disguise
Explain the Metropolis rule and why it samples the target
Tune a sampler's step size and spot a chain that's stuck

sections.title: A walk that remembers only now

blocks.html:
A Markov chain is a random process where the next state depends only on the current one, not on the whole history. Tomorrow's weather given today's. A shopper's next aisle given this one. Your next word given the last.

That short memory is surprisingly powerful. Let it run long enough and it often settles into a fixed long-run pattern. And you can design a chain whose long-run pattern is whatever distribution you want. That's MCMC, Markov chain Monte Carlo, the engine behind modern Bayesian statistics.

blocks.name: ps-mcmc
blocks.title: A walker that samples two islands
blocks.goal: Get the mismatch below 0.10 after at least 6,000 steps (you'll need to change the step size).
blocks.intro: Grey glass is the shape we want to sample. The amber walker follows the Metropolis rule; blue columns count where it has been.

blocks.q: With step size 1 the walker stayed on the left island. Why?

opts.t: The right island has less probability
Every small step into the valley is a big drop in height, so it's nearly always refused; small steps can't reach the other island
The walker is programmed to stay where it started
Step size 1 means it never moves

blocks.why: The chain is still correct in theory, it would get there eventually, but "eventually" could be millions of steps. Real samplers fail like this all the time, which is why people run several chains from different starting points and check they agree.

blocks.html: Put the chances in a table: row = today, column = tomorrow. Each row adds to 1. If d is today's distribution (a row vector), tomorrow's is d @ P.

blocks.code:
P = np.array([[0.9, 0.1],     # sunny -> sunny, rainy
              [0.5, 0.5]])    # rainy -> sunny, rainy
d = np.array([0.0, 1.0])      # it's raining today
for day in range(1, 4):
    d = d @ P
    print(day, d.round(3))

blocks.html: The chain is forgetting that it started on a rainy day. Where does it end up?

blocks.html: Most chains forget their start and settle into a stationary distribution π with π @ P = π. For the weather chain, it's sunny 5/6 of the time in the long run, whatever today is. One way to find π: start anywhere and keep stepping until it stops changing (power iteration).

blocks.html:
Early Google ranked pages with a Markov chain. Imagine a surfer who, on each page, clicks a random link with probability 0.85, or gets bored and jumps to a random page with probability 0.15. The stationary distribution of that walk is the PageRank: pages that lots of important pages link to get visited a lot.

The random jump matters: without it the surfer could get trapped on a page with no links out, and the chain would never settle.

Now flip the problem. We have a shape p(x) we can evaluate (say prior × likelihood from chapter 11) and we want samples from it. Metropolis builds a chain whose stationary distribution is exactly p:

  1. from the current x, propose x′ = x + a small random step;
  2. if p(x′) ≥ p(x), move there;
  3. otherwise move there with probability p(x′) / p(x), else stay at x (and record x again).

You only ever need the ratio p(x′) / p(x), so the unknown normalising total cancels out. That's why it's so useful.

blocks.q: A sampler accepts 99% of its proposals. What's the likely problem?

opts.t: Nothing, a high acceptance rate is ideal
The steps are tiny, so it barely moves and explores very slowly
The steps are huge
The target distribution is wrong

blocks.why: Tiny steps are almost always accepted because the height barely changes, but the walker crawls. Huge steps are mostly rejected. A common rule of thumb for one-dimensional targets is to aim for roughly 40–50% acceptance, and lower in many dimensions.

blocks.q: Explain what a stationary distribution is and how the Metropolis rule uses it to draw samples from a shape you can't sample directly.
blocks.a: A Markov chain hops between states using only the current state. Many chains settle into a long-run pattern where the fraction of time in each state stops changing: that's the stationary distribution, π @ P = π. Metropolis designs a chain whose stationary distribution is the target: propose a nearby point, always accept if it's higher, accept with probability new/old if it's lower. Only ratios of heights are needed, so unknown normalising constants cancel. Run it long enough and the time spent in each region matches the target; but if steps are too small or too big it explores slowly, so you check acceptance rates and run several chains.
